info.desc: Blur is the fifth album by English alternative rock band Blur. Released on 10 February 1997 in the UK, it reached the top of the UK album chart. Blur was also a hit in the US, with Song 2 becoming a hit there and the album being certified Gold. It also spawned several hit singles in the UK, most notably Beetlebum and "Song 2". The album's style was resultant of Blur's dropping their previous Britpop mantle after The Great Escape in favor of lo-fi and alternative rock recordings, reportedly at Graham Coxon 's urging. podcast.body: Recorded outside the United Kingdom, this album marked Blur's definitive departure from the Britpop movement at its peak. It is considered a masterpiece with a lo-fi sound, and through it, Blur expressed a desire to completely distance themselves from anything related to Britpop. It's a curious case where the band that spearheaded the transition and entered the golden age of Britpop was also the first to abandon it.

Released in February 1997, this self-titled album signaled a new sonic path for the band, marking a "stunning aesthetic reversal" led by Damon Albarn. It was decidedly not Britpop, showcasing Albarn's new fascinations with low-fi American alternative music, obscure 1970s German progressive rock, and Sub-Saharan African music. "This was not Britpop."

podcast.body: The self-titled album marked a deliberate shift away from the band's Britpop sound, influenced by Graham Coxon's deep dive into American indie and lo-fi bands like Pavement. This change in direction was widely accepted by the band members, resulting in a distinctly different sound for their fifth record. "Weirdly, just about everyone agreed with him, which is why the fifth Blur record sounded so different than the Brit pop stuff that came before it."

podcast.title: Self-Titled
podcast.body: The recording of this self-titled album by Blur was influenced by Radiohead's *The Bends*. Damon Albarn cited *The Bends* as a reason for Blur to abandon the classic Britpop style and explore new sounds. "decía que una de las razones que les empujó abandonar la estela clásica del Britpop era precisamente el álbum de Benz de Radiohead que les había hecho un poco darse cuenta de que había que ir a buscar sonidos nuevos."
